definition: Believing that people act mainly out of selfishness and distrusting the reasons they give.
example: After years of broken promises, she grew cynical about the landlord's offers to fix the heat.
nuance: A skeptic doubts a claim until there is evidence; a cynic assumes the worst about people's motives from the start.
prompt: A neighbor offers to help a family move their furniture for free.
options: Her cynical brother assumed the neighbor secretly wanted something in return.
Her cynical brother was certain the offer came from pure kindness and nothing else.
The neighbor's help was cynical, returning every spring like the robins.
The cynical boxes sat stacked in neat rows beside the front door.
reasons: Suspecting a hidden selfish motive behind a kind offer is exactly the cynic's outlook.
Trusting that a motive is wholly generous is the opposite of a cynic's suspicion.
This confuses the word with cyclical, which describes something that repeats in a pattern.
Cardboard boxes hold no beliefs about anyone's motives, so they cannot be distrustful.

practice.prompt: A bakery announces it will donate its leftover bread to a local shelter.
options: The donations were cynical, recurring on the same morning every week.
A cynical customer muttered that the owners only wanted good publicity.
A cynical customer cheered, convinced the owners were acting out of generosity alone.
The cynical loaves were still warm when the delivery van pulled up.
reasons: Repeating on a schedule describes something cyclical, a look-alike word with another meaning.
Dismissing a generous act as a bid for attention shows distrust of people's motives.
Wholehearted faith in someone's good intentions reverses what the word means.
Bread has no attitude toward human motives; the word describes a person's outlook.
